The High Holy Days. The most solemn period in the Jewish calendar, consisting primarily of Rosh Hashanah and Yom Kippur, observances in the autumn that focus on repentance, reflection, and spiritual renewal. The ten-day period known as the Days of Awe is considered the most important season in Judaism, when believers seek forgiveness from God and from fellow humans. These days center on themes of judgment, atonement, and recommitment to Jewish law and values.

Rosh Hashanah, meaning Head of the Year, marks the Jewish New Year and commemorates the creation of the world in Jewish tradition. Yom Kippur, or Day of Atonement, is observed as the holiest day in Judaism, a day of complete fasting and intensive prayer for forgiveness. The ten days between them are known as the Days of Repentance or Days of Awe, devoted to spiritual introspection and amendment.

Jewish tradition teaches that on Rosh Hashanah, God judges all beings, with final judgment sealed on Yom Kippur, and sincere repentance can overturn harsh decree. During the High Holy Days, Jews confess sins, recite special prayers called piyyutim, and engage in acts of charity to demonstrate sincere repentance. These holidays suspend normal work and creative activities, with the entire community gathering in synagogue for extended services emphasizing prayer over ritual action, connecting these days to Judaism itself and to broader themes of repentance that define Jewish spiritual life.
